tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The match starts at seven." → "She said the match started at seven."
Direct: "Where is the bus stop?" → "He asked where was the bus stop."
Direct: "We will bake bread tomorrow." → "They said they will bake bread tomorrow."
Direct: "Did you lock the bike?" → "She asked if I had locked the bike."
Direct: "I finished the essay yesterday." → "He said he had finished the essay yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After a past reporting verb, present simple backshifts to past simple: "starts" becomes "started."

Tip: Past said/asked usually pulls the reported verb one step back in time.

FALSE — Embedded wh-questions keep statement order: subject before the verb. "Where was the bus stop?" is still direct-question order.

Tip: Use "where the bus stop was," not "where was…"

FALSE — "Will" normally backshifts to "would," and "tomorrow" usually becomes "the next day."

Tip: "They said they would bake bread the next day."

TRUE — Yes/no questions take if/whether plus statement order, and past simple often becomes past perfect.

Tip: "asked if/whether + subject + had + past participle."

FALSE — Time markers shift with the tense: "yesterday" becomes "the day before" (or "the previous day").

Tip: Pair backshift with deictic shifts: yesterday → the day before; tomorrow → the next day.
tasks.solution_overview: This set drills the core trio: tense backshift after said/asked, statement word order in embedded questions, and shifting time markers like yesterday. Mark each line as a legal report of the given direct speech — or not.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I can swim across the lake." → "She said she can swim across the lake."
Direct: "When does the museum open?" → "He asked when the museum opened."
Direct: "We must pack today." → "She said they had to pack that day."
Direct: "I have watered the plants." → "He said he had watered the plants."
Direct: "Are the tickets ready?" → "She asked are the tickets ready."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Ability "can" typically backshifts to "could" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: "She said she could swim across the lake."

TRUE — Wh-word stays, tense backshifts, and the clause keeps subject–verb statement order.

Tip: "asked when + subject + past verb," never "when does/did…"

TRUE — Obligation "must" often becomes "had to," and "today" shifts to "that day."

Tip: Present obligation markers (must/today) usually reshape in past reports.

TRUE — Present perfect backshifts cleanly to past perfect after said.

Tip: have/has + past participle → had + past participle.

FALSE — Reported yes/no questions need if/whether and statement order, not inverted "are the tickets…"

Tip: "She asked whether the tickets were ready."
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on modal backshift (can → could, must → had to), present perfect → past perfect, and the if/whether pattern for yes/no reports. Embedded wh-questions should already feel like statements.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The choir rehearses here tomorrow." → "He said the choir rehearsed here tomorrow."
Direct: "Why did the neighbour leave?" → "She asked why did the neighbour leave."
Direct: "I am reading the novel now." → "He said he was reading the novel then."
Direct: "Do not feed the stray cats." → "She told me do not feed the stray cats."
Direct: "We may hike next weekend." → "They said they may hike next weekend."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Place and time markers usually shift: "here" → "there," "tomorrow" → "the next day" / "the following day."

Tip: "He said the choir rehearsed there the following day."

FALSE — Embedded why-questions need statement order and usually past-perfect backshift: not "why did the neighbour…"

Tip: "She asked why the neighbour had left."

TRUE — Present continuous backshifts to past continuous, and "now" becomes "then."

Tip: am/is/are + -ing → was/were + -ing; now → then.

FALSE — Negative commands in reports use told/asked + object + not + to-infinitive.

Tip: "She told me not to feed the stray cats."

FALSE — "May" for possibility often becomes "might," and "next weekend" should become "the following weekend."

Tip: "They said they might hike the following weekend."
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps stack deictics, leftover do-support, unshifted may/next, and a bare negative command. Only the continuous now→then line is clean.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Please text me the address." → "He asked me to text him the address."
Direct: "Who watered the garden?" → "She asked who had watered the garden."
Direct: "I will have finished by Friday." → "He said he would have finished by Friday."
Direct: "This recipe needs more salt." → "She said that recipe needed more salt."
Direct: "Have you seen my keys?" → "He asked had I seen his keys."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Polite requests report as asked + object + to-infinitive.

Tip: Direct "Please…" → "asked someone to…"

TRUE — Subject questions keep who as subject; the tense still backshifts.

Tip: "asked who had watered…" is statement-like and correctly shifted.

TRUE — Future perfect "will have finished" backshifts to "would have finished."

Tip: will → would even inside perfect constructions.

TRUE — "This" often becomes "that" after a past report, with present → past.

Tip: Demonstratives move with the reporting frame.

FALSE — Yes/no perfect questions need if/whether + statement order, not "had I…" inversion.

Tip: "He asked whether I had seen his keys."
tasks.solution_overview: Four solid reports cover requests, subject questions, future perfect backshift, and this→that. The trap is leftover question inversion after asked.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "The soup is too salty." → "Mia told that the soup was too salty."
Direct: "How long have you lived here?" → "She asked how long I had lived there."
Direct: "We shall meet at noon." → "He said they should meet at noon."
Direct: "I saw the fox last night." → "She said she had seen the fox the night before."
Direct: "Can you join the hike?" → "He asked could I join the hike."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Tell" needs a personal object: tell someone that…; without an object, use "said that…"

Tip: said that / told us that — never bare "told that."

TRUE — Present perfect → past perfect, "here" → "there," and statement order after how long.

Tip: Bundle tense, place, and order shifts together.

TRUE — Formal "shall" for future often reports as "should" (or "would") after past said.

Tip: Treat shall like will when backshifting future meaning.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect and "last night" → "the night before."

Tip: Relative past time phrases shift just like yesterday/tomorrow.

FALSE — Modal yes/no reports need if/whether + subject + could, not "could I…" inversion.

Tip: "He asked if I could join the hike."
tasks.solution_overview: Say versus tell joins the usual backshift package. Watch for missing objects after tell and for inverted modals after asked.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Bring a spare towel." → "She told us to bring a spare towel."
Direct: "I may be late." → "He said he might be late."
Direct: "Where have they put the map?" → "She asked where they had put the map."
Direct: "We were discussing the film." → "He said they had been discussing the film."
Direct: "I leave for Lisbon tonight." → "She said she was leaving for Lisbon that night."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Imperatives report as tell/ask + object + to-infinitive.

Tip: Command verb drops; to + base verb carries the instruction.

TRUE — Possibility "may" commonly becomes "might" in past reports.

Tip: may → might is the safe exam backshift.

TRUE — Wh-word + statement order + present perfect → past perfect.

Tip: "asked where they had put…" — no auxiliary before the subject.

TRUE — Past continuous often becomes past perfect continuous after a past reporting verb.

Tip: was/were + -ing → had been + -ing when sequence needs a further step back.

TRUE — Present simple for a near arrangement can report as past continuous, with "tonight" → "that night."

Tip: Timetabled or arranged futures often surface as was/were + -ing in reports.
tasks.solution_overview: All five lines are clean reports: commands with to-infinitive, modal may→might, embedded perfect questions, past continuous deepening, and arranged-future reporting.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I must have left my scarf at the café." → "He said he must have left his scarf at the café."
Direct: "Will the library renew the card?" → "She asked would the library renew the card."
Direct: "These clouds are gathering." → "He said those clouds were gathering."
Direct: "I used to cycle to school." → "She said she used to cycle to school."
Direct: "Don't forget the tickets." → "He reminded me not to forget the tickets."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Deduction "must have" often stays unchanged because it already refers to a past conclusion.

Tip: Logical deduction with must have need not backshift further.

FALSE — Yes/no with will needs if/whether + would + subject, not "would the library…" inversion.

Tip: "She asked whether the library would renew the card."

TRUE — "These" → "those" and present continuous → past continuous.

Tip: Demonstratives shift with the reporting viewpoint.

TRUE — "Used to" already marks past habit and normally stays as used to after said.

Tip: No further backshift is required for used to.

TRUE — Negative reminders use not + to-infinitive after remind/tell.

Tip: "reminded me not to forget…" mirrors "told me not to…"
tasks.solution_overview: Some forms resist further shift (must have, used to); others still demand if/whether and statement order. Separate "leave alone" cases from order traps.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Why are you delaying the trip?" → "She asked why were we delaying the trip."
Direct: "I ought to call my sister." → "He said he ought to call his sister."
Direct: "We arrived two days ago." → "They said they had arrived two days ago."
Direct: "Is this the final draft?" → "He asked if that was the final draft."
Direct: "I will phone you later today." → "She said she would phone me later that day."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Keep statement order: "why we were delaying," not "why were we…"

Tip: After asked, never reinvert the auxiliary before the subject.

TRUE — "Ought to" typically remains ought to in reported speech.

Tip: Ought to is already modal-like and usually does not change form.

FALSE — "Ago" normally becomes "before" / "earlier" in past reports; keeping "ago" clashes with the shifted frame.

Tip: "They said they had arrived two days before."

TRUE — Yes/no with if, this→that, and present→past all apply together.

Tip: Bundle if + demonstrative shift + tense shift.

TRUE — will→would and today→that day after past said.

Tip: Future markers and same-day time words both move.
tasks.solution_overview: The hard spots are inverted wh-clauses and leftover "ago." Ought to and clean if/that/will shifts show the correct pattern.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "We need not renew the membership yet." → "She said they need not renew the membership yet."
Direct: "What time does the ferry leave?" → "He asked what time the ferry left."
Direct: "I have been waiting since Monday." → "She said she had been waiting since Monday."
Direct: "Come back the day after tomorrow." → "They told us to come back in two days' time."
Direct: "I can't approve this design." → "He said he couldn't approve that design."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Need not" for lack of obligation often stays need not (or becomes did not need to).

Tip: Either unchanged need not or did not need to is acceptable; bare "needed not" is wrong.

TRUE — Wh-clause with statement order and present→past.

Tip: "asked what time + subject + past verb."

TRUE — Present perfect continuous backshifts to past perfect continuous.

Tip: have/has been + -ing → had been + -ing.

TRUE — "The day after tomorrow" can paraphrase as "in two days' time" / "two days later."

Tip: Distant relative time phrases are often reworded, not left literal.

TRUE — can→could and this→that in one tidy report.

Tip: Modal ability and demonstratives usually shift together after past said.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are acceptable advanced reports: need not, embedded timetable questions, perfect continuous backshift, reworded far-future time, and can/this shifts.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Who did you invite?" → "She asked who did I invite."
Direct: "The cherries ripened last year." → "He said the cherries had ripened the year before."
Direct: "Shall I postpone the picnic?" → "She asked if she should postpone the picnic."
Direct: "We are going to plant lavender." → "They said they were going to plant lavender."
Direct: "I won't leave until Friday." → "He said he won't leave until Friday."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Object questions drop do-support and use statement order: "who I had invited."

Tip: After asked, no "did" before the subject.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect and "last year" → "the year before."

Tip: Calendar "last…" phrases become "the … before / previous …"

TRUE — Offer/suggestion shall I… reports as if/whether + should.

Tip: "asked if she should…" is the standard mapping.

TRUE — "Be going to" backshifts was/were going to after past said.

Tip: Treat going-to futures like other present forms that shift one step.

FALSE — "Won't" should become "wouldn't" after a past reporting verb.

Tip: will/won't → would/wouldn't in standard backshift.
tasks.solution_overview: Object-question do-support and unshifted won't are the failures. Going-to futures, shall→should offers, and last-year time shifts are the models.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide said, "Water freezes at zero," and later reported that water freezes at zero.
Direct: "Could you pass the salt?" → "She asked me if I could pass the salt."
Direct: "I was cooking when the power failed." → "He said he had been cooking when the power had failed."
Direct: "Whose umbrella is this?" → "He asked whose umbrella was this."
Direct: "We needn't have brought extra chairs." → "She said they needn't have brought extra chairs."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — When the situation is still true, some writers keep present tense after a past report; it is acceptable for ongoing facts.

Tip: Backshift is usual but not compulsory for permanently or still-valid truths.

TRUE — Polite could you… can report as asked + if + could + statement order.

Tip: Ability/request could often stays could inside if-clauses.

FALSE — Over-shifting both verbs to past perfect can distort simultaneous past events; keep the time-clause past simple if it marks the interrupting moment.

Tip: Prefer "had been cooking when the power failed."

FALSE — Statement order needed: "whose umbrella this was," not "whose umbrella was this."

Tip: Possessive wh-questions still lose inversion in reports.

TRUE — "Needn't have" for unnecessary past action commonly remains needn't have.

Tip: Perfect modal forms for past comments often stay put.
tasks.solution_overview: Optional non-backshift for still-true facts sits beside over-shifted time clauses and inverted whose-questions. Perfect need not and polite could-if reports are fine.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Let's postpone the rehearsal." → "She suggested postponing the rehearsal."
Direct: "I wish I knew the answer." → "He said he wished he knew the answer."
Direct: "Had you finished before the storm?" → "She asked whether I had finished before the storm."
Direct: "We thrived here last spring." → "They said they had thrived there the previous spring."
Direct: "You had better rest." → "He said I had better rest."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Let's…" suggestions often report as suggested + gerund (or suggested that…).

Tip: Suggest takes a gerund or a that-clause, not bare to-infinitive without that.

TRUE — Wish-clauses already sit in a past-like form; reporting them usually keeps wished + past form.

Tip: Do not force a further unnatural backshift inside wish.

TRUE — Past perfect yes/no questions report with if/whether + had + past participle and statement order.

Tip: Inversion from the direct Had you… disappears after asked.

TRUE — Past simple → past perfect plus here→there and last→previous.

Tip: Stack place and calendar shifts with the tense change.

TRUE — "Had better" for advice typically remains had better after said.

Tip: Had better does not become would better.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line is a valid report: let's→suggest + -ing, wish retention, whether + past perfect, stacked deictics, and unchanged had better.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I would rather stay indoors." → "She said she would rather stayed indoors."
Direct: "When will you publish the photos?" → "He asked when we would publish the photos."
Direct: "I might have misread the map." → "He said he might have misread the map."
Direct: "Stay where you are." → "Security told us to stay where we were."
Direct: "Did the nurse call you yesterday?" → "She asked if the nurse had called me yesterday."
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After would rather, keep the base verb: "would rather stay," not "stayed."

Tip: Would rather + bare infinitive survives reporting.

TRUE — will→would inside a wh-clause with statement order.

Tip: "asked when + subject + would + verb."

TRUE — "Might have" for past possibility usually stays might have.

Tip: Perfect modals of speculation rarely need further change.

TRUE — Imperative plus embedded where-clause: to-infinitive outside, backshift inside the where-clause.

Tip: "to stay where we were" — both layers handled.

FALSE — "Yesterday" should become "the day before" once the reporting verb is past.

Tip: "…had called me the day before."
tasks.solution_overview: Would rather keeps a base verb; yesterday still must shift. Wh-future reports, might have, and nested where-clauses show controlled backshift.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I insist that the lyrics be rewritten." → "She insisted that the lyrics be rewritten."
Direct: "How much did the festival cost?" → "He asked how much the festival had cost."
Direct: "We will be launching next Monday." → "They said they would be launching the following Monday."
Direct: "I never said that." → "She claimed she had never said that."
Direct: "Are you being serious?" → "He asked if I was being serious."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Formal mandative subjunctive after insist often stays be + past participle in the report.

Tip: Reporting insist that… can preserve the base-form subjunctive.

TRUE — Object how-much questions drop did and backshift to past perfect with statement order.

Tip: "asked how much + subject + had + past participle."

TRUE — Future continuous will be + -ing → would be + -ing, and next → the following.

Tip: Progressive futures backshift the will piece only.

TRUE — Past simple negation becomes past perfect in a past report when the earlier speech act is prior.

Tip: "had never said" places the denial further back.

TRUE — Present continuous being → past continuous being after if.

Tip: "asked if I was being…" — statement order, tense shifted.
highlights: how much the festival had cost
tasks.solution_overview: All five succeed: preserved mandative be, cleaned object questions, future continuous backshift, prior-speech past perfect, and continuous being after if.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I would have called if I had known." → "She said she would have called if she had known."
Direct: "Which shelf holds the spices?" → "He asked which shelf did hold the spices."
Direct: "The offer expires the day after tomorrow." → "They said the offer expired two days later."
Direct: "Must we disclose the allergy?" → "She asked if they had to disclose the allergy."
Direct: "I am to present at nine." → "He said he was to present at nine."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Conditional perfect forms already sit far back and typically stay would have / had + past participle when reported.

Tip: Do not invent an extra layer beyond would have + past perfect.

FALSE — No do-support in the embedded clause: "which shelf held the spices."

Tip: Wh-determiners keep statement order without did.

TRUE — "The day after tomorrow" → "two days later" / "in two days" is a natural time rewrite.

Tip: Far deixis is often paraphrased in polished reports.

TRUE — Obligation must in questions often becomes had to after asked if.

Tip: "asked if they had to…" is the usual mapping.

TRUE — Formal "be to" for scheduled duty backshifts was/were to.

Tip: am/is/are to → was/were to after past said.
tasks.solution_overview: One illegal did in a which-clause breaks the set. Elsewhere, remote conditionals, time paraphrase, must→had to, and be-to schedules report cleanly.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "You needn't worry about the weather." → "He told me I didn't need to worry about the weather."
Direct: "Whereabouts is the camping stove?" → "She asked whereabouts was the camping stove."
Direct: "I have got to leave now." → "He said he had got to leave then."
Direct: "We shall have completed the mural by June." → "They said they would have completed the mural by June."
Direct: "Why must the window stay open?" → "She asked why the window had to stay open."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Needn't" can report as didn't need to / needn't after a past frame.

Tip: Personal object after told plus shifted lack-of-obligation form.

FALSE — Even with whereabouts, keep statement order: "whereabouts the camping stove was."

Tip: Any wh-word still bans auxiliary-before-subject after asked.

TRUE — "Have got to" obligation backshifts to had got to, and now→then.

Tip: Treat have got to like must for backshift purposes.

TRUE — shall have + past participle (future perfect) → would have + past participle.

Tip: Future perfect always yields would have in standard past reports.

TRUE — why + must → why + had to with statement order.

Tip: Obligation questions lose must inversion and often become had to.
tasks.solution_overview: Whereabouts inversion is the sole fault. Needn't→didn't need to, have got to, future perfect, and why-must→had to are sound.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Were the paths cleared last winter?" → "She asked whether the paths had been cleared the previous winter."
Direct: "I would prefer you not to spoil this yet." → "She said she would prefer us not to spoil that yet."
Direct: "Dare I ask for a refund?" → "He asked if he dared ask for a refund."
Direct: "The team will have been rehearsing for six hours by then." → "She said the team would have been rehearsing for six hours by then."
Direct: "What if we delay the concert?" → "He asked what if we delayed the concert."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Passive past yes/no → whether + past perfect passive + last→previous.

Tip: Voice stays passive; only tense and time words move.

TRUE — Would prefer + object + not to stays structurally; pronouns and this→that adjust.

Tip: Preference patterns largely keep their skeleton under reporting.

TRUE — Rare dare questions can report as if + dared + bare infinitive.

Tip: Modal-like dare often becomes a past lexical dare in reports.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing.

Tip: Only will becomes would; the rest of the stack stays.

TRUE — "What if…" hypotheticals often keep what if and simply backshift the following verb.

Tip: "asked what if we delayed…" is natural exam English.
highlights: had been cleared the previous winter
tasks.solution_overview: A clean advanced sweep: passive perfect reports, prefer + not to, dare, future perfect continuous, and what-if backshift — all grammatical.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Seldom have we seen such fog." → "She said seldom had they seen such fog."
Direct: "I was to have signed before noon." → "He said he was to have signed before noon."
Direct: "Who should we notify first?" → "She asked who should we notify first."
Direct: "The bread will still be warm tomorrow morning." → "He said the bread would still be warm the next morning."
Direct: "Might the shop extend its hours?" → "They asked might the shop extend its hours."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Negative inversion can survive inside the reported clause after said, with pronoun and tense already matching.

Tip: Reporting rare inverted rhetoric may keep the inverted shape.

TRUE — "Was to have + past participle" (unfulfilled plan) typically remains was to have…

Tip: This past-scheduled perfect form needs no further shift.

FALSE — Embedded object questions need statement order: "who we should notify first."

Tip: Modal should still follows the subject after asked.

TRUE — Future will → would, and tomorrow morning → the next morning.

Tip: Will and time words move together after past said.

FALSE — Yes/no might needs if/whether + subject + might, not "might the shop…"

Tip: "They asked whether the shop might extend…"
tasks.solution_overview: Inverted who-should and bare might-yes/no fail. Surviving rhetorical inversion, was-to-have, and would + next-morning time shifts are acceptable.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "I'd rather you didn't spoil this." → "She said she'd rather I didn't spoil that."
Direct: "How come the cake collapsed?" → "He asked how come the cake had collapsed."
Direct: "We used not to skip breakfast." → "They said they used not to skip breakfast."
Direct: "Will you have finished by the time I call?" → "She asked if I would have finished by the time she called."
Direct: "Suppose we freeze the leftovers." → "He suggested that we freeze the leftovers."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Would rather + past clause for preference about someone else keeps that past shape; this→that adjusts.

Tip: Preferential rather-clauses are not forced into past perfect.

TRUE — Informal how come reports with statement order and optional past perfect for a prior failure.

Tip: "asked how come + subject + (had) + past participle."

TRUE — "Used not to" (or didn't use to) for past habit can remain used not to.

Tip: Habitual used to patterns are already past-oriented.

TRUE — Future perfect in a yes/no question → if + would have, and the time-clause present→past.

Tip: Both the main future perfect and the by-the-time clause shift.

TRUE — Suppose-ideas often become suggested that + base or past form in formal reports.

Tip: Mandative or tentative freeze after suggested that is exam-friendly.
highlights: how come the cake had collapsed
tasks.solution_overview: All five are advanced but valid: rather + past clause, how come, used not to, nested would-have with by-the-time, and suggested that.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Direct: "Not only is the path steep, but the wind is fierce." → "She said not only was the path steep, but the wind was fierce."
Direct: "I needn't have packed every jumper." → "He said he needn't have packed every jumper."
Direct: "Where should the chairs sit?" → "She asked where should the chairs sit."
Direct: "By next March we will have been leasing the studio for a decade." → "They said that by the following March they would have been leasing the studio for a decade."
Direct: "Was anyone monitoring the feed then?" → "She asked was anyone monitoring the feed then."
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Correlative not only…but also can keep inversion after said while tenses sit in the past.

Tip: Reporting flashy inversion is optional but grammatical if pronouns and tenses align.

TRUE — Needn't have for unnecessary past action stays needn't have.

Tip: Perfect absence-of-need does not become hadn't need.

FALSE — Statement order required: "where the chairs should sit."

Tip: Modal should follows the subject in embedded wh-questions.

TRUE — next→the following and will have been + -ing → would have been + -ing.

Tip: Long future-perfect-continuous stacks only change will→would.

FALSE — Yes/no past continuous needs if/whether + statement order: "whether anyone was monitoring…"

Tip: Never leave bare "was anyone…" after asked.
tasks.solution_overview: Two order failures remain: should after where, and bare was-anyone after asked. Inverted not only, needn't have, and future perfect continuous reports are fine.
